├── lindera-binding/        # FFI-independent helpers shared by the language bindings
├── lindera-ipadic/         # IPADIC dictionary (Japanese)
├── lindera-ipadic-neologd/ # IPADIC NEologd dictionary (Japanese)
├── lindera-unidic/         # UniDic dictionary (Japanese)
├── lindera-sudachidict/    # SudachiDict dictionary (Japanese)
├── lindera-ko-dic/         # ko-dic dictionary (Korean)
├── lindera-cc-cedict/      # CC-CEDICT dictionary (Chinese)
├── lindera-jieba/          # Jieba dictionary (Chinese)
├── lindera-python/         # Python bindings (PyO3)
├── lindera-nodejs/         # Node.js bindings (NAPI-RS)
├── lindera-ruby/           # Ruby bindings (Magnus + rb-sys)
├── lindera-php/            # PHP bindings (ext-php-rs)
├── lindera-wasm/           # WebAssembly bindings (wasm-bindgen)
├── resources/              # Test resources and sample data
└── docs/                   # Documentation (mdBook)

Crate Descriptions

Core Crates

lindera-crf

Pure Rust implementation of Conditional Random Fields (CRF). Supports no_std environments. Uses rkyv for fast zero-copy serialization. This crate provides the statistical learning engine used in dictionary training.

lindera-dictionary

Base library for dictionary handling: loading, building, and querying dictionaries.

lindera-trainer

CRF training pipeline for creating custom dictionaries. Builds on lindera-dictionary runtime types and the lindera-crf engine. Consumed through the lindera facade's train feature (re-exported as lindera::dictionary::trainer).

ModuleRole
config.rsConfiguration management (seed dict, char.def, feature.def, rewrite.def)
corpus.rsTraining corpus processing
feature_extractor.rsFeature template parsing and feature ID management
feature_rewriter.rsMeCab-compatible feature rewriting (3-section format)
model.rsTrained model storage, serialization, and dictionary output

lindera-segmenter

The morphological segmentation library (published as lindera up to v6). Integrates the dictionary crates and provides the Segmenter API. Its dictionary module also re-exports the raw lindera-dictionary modules (builder, core, loader, viterbi, ...).

lindera

The facade crate and the single dependency for Rust users. It re-exports every module of lindera-segmenter and, with the default analysis feature, lindera-analysis as lindera::analysis. The directory also holds the integration tests, examples, and benches that exercise the public paths.

lindera-analysis

Lucene-style analysis chain on top of lindera-segmenter (used as lindera::analysis through the facade): character filters, token filters, and the Tokenizer that composes them around a Segmenter.

lindera-cli

Command-line interface for tokenization, dictionary training, export, and building. The train feature is enabled by default.

lindera-binding

FFI-independent helpers shared by all five language bindings (lindera-python, lindera-nodejs, lindera-ruby, lindera-php, lindera-wasm): a core tokenizer/schema/metadata layer that each binding wraps in its own language-native API. It depends on the lindera facade.

Dictionary Crates

Each dictionary crate contains pre-built dictionary data for a specific language and dictionary source.

CrateLanguageDictionary Source
lindera-ipadicJapaneseIPADIC
lindera-ipadic-neologdJapaneseIPADIC NEologd (extended vocabulary)
lindera-unidicJapaneseUniDic
lindera-sudachidictJapaneseSudachiDict
lindera-ko-dicKoreanko-dic
lindera-cc-cedictChineseCC-CEDICT
lindera-jiebaChineseJieba

Bindings

lindera-python

Python bindings built with PyO3. Exposes the Lindera tokenizer API to Python applications.

lindera-nodejs

Node.js bindings built with NAPI-RS. Exposes the Lindera tokenizer API to Node.js applications.

lindera-ruby

Ruby bindings built with Magnus and rb-sys. Exposes the Lindera tokenizer API as a Ruby gem.

lindera-php

PHP bindings built with ext-php-rs. Exposes the Lindera tokenizer API as a PHP extension. The extension registers as lindera and is published on Packagist as lindera/lindera for PIE: the package's composer.json lives at the repository root and points PIE at lindera-php/, where config.m4 and Makefile.frag drive cargo build through the phpize build.

lindera-wasm

WebAssembly bindings built with wasm-bindgen. Enables tokenization in browsers and Node.js.

Other Directories

resources/

Test resources including sample dictionaries, user dictionaries, and test corpora used by the test suite.

docs/

User-facing documentation built with mdBook. The table of contents is defined in docs/src/SUMMARY.md. A Japanese translation is available under docs/ja/.

lindera/examples/ and lindera-analysis/examples/

Runnable example programs demonstrating common usage patterns. Run with:

cargo run -p lindera --features=embed-ipadic --example=segment
cargo run -p lindera-analysis --features=embed-ipadic --example=tokenize

Training Pipeline

Lindera provides CRF-based dictionary training functionality for creating custom morphological analysis models. This feature requires the train feature flag.

Overview

The training pipeline follows three stages:

lindera train --> model.dat --> lindera export --> dictionary files --> lindera build --> compiled dictionary
  1. Train: Learn CRF weights from an annotated corpus and seed dictionary, producing a binary model file.
  2. Export: Convert the trained model into Lindera dictionary source files.
  3. Build: Compile the source files into a binary dictionary that Lindera can load at runtime.

How training works

lindera train builds one lattice for each sentence of the corpus, as MeCab's learner does. At every position, the lattice has the seed words that start there and the unknown words that the runtime creates there from char.def and unk.def (see Character Definition and Unknown Word Definition). The CRF learns the weights that make the annotated path, the gold tokens, the cheapest. Each gold token is labelled with the first of these that fits:

  1. The first seed row, in file order, with the same span and the same whole feature string. Unlike MeCab's learner, which compares only the first eval-size columns, every column must match, so a token whose reading or other columns differ from the seed row falls through to the next steps.
  2. The first unk.def entry, in file order, of an unknown-word candidate with the same span whose feature columns other than * all equal the gold token's columns.
  3. A virtual label built from the gold feature string, as MeCab's learner adds a virtual node. Gold tokens with the same feature string share one virtual label. Virtual labels are trained but not exported.

Every other candidate is a negative example. Once the lattices are built, lindera train prints how the gold tokens were labelled; with the files in resources/training/:

Lattice statistics: gold_lexicon=14 gold_unknown=0 gold_virtual=0 virtual_labels=0 negative_lexicon=0 negative_unknown=17

gold_lexicon, gold_unknown and gold_virtual count the gold tokens labelled by each of the three steps, virtual_labels counts the virtual labels, and negative_lexicon and negative_unknown count the negative edges from the seed lexicon and from the unknown-word candidates.

A seed row that no gold token is labelled with is only ever a negative example. So lindera train warns on standard error when no gold token is a seed word, or when fewer than half of the gold tokens whose surface has seed rows are seed words, as when the corpus does not give its gold tokens the feature strings of the seed rows. The warning shows the first gold token whose surface has seed rows but none with its feature string, next to the feature strings of the first five of those rows, and training goes on. For example, with every feature of resources/training/corpus.txt cut to its first six columns, without the base form and the readings:

Warning: 0 of the 14 gold tokens are seed words, and 14 are not although seed rows have their surface. A gold token is a seed word only when a seed row has its surface and its whole feature string, as the seed lexicon writes it; otherwise the seed rows with its surface are only wrong candidates at its position. The first such gold token, and the seed rows with its surface:
  gold token: 外国	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*
  seed row:   外国	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,外国,ガイコク,ガイコク

Gold tokens whose surface no seed row has do not count toward the warning, so a seed lexicon that covers little of the corpus gives none.

The CRF is then trained with L-BFGS (OWL-QN when the regularization has an L1 part). As in MeCab's learner and libLBFGS, the first line search starts at a step of 1 / |d|, d being the first search direction, so that its first trial point lies at unit distance from the initial weights, and every later one at a step of 1 (#1290). Training stops at the first of these:

  • converged: the relative change of the objective, |previous - current| / |previous|, stayed below eta for 3 iterations in a row. The default eta is that of MeCab's learner, which applies the same test to every evaluation, line-search trials included, where Lindera counts iterations. Training also converged when it stopped in either of the two ways below near the optimum, where the norm of the gradient is under 1e-5 times its norm at the initial weights: there the objective changes by less than its rounding, and which of the two comes first depends on the platform (#1300).
  • no progress: an iteration left the objective unchanged far from the optimum, where the norm of the gradient was still at least 1e-5 times its norm at the initial weights. When this happens after a few iterations, the model is barely trained. lindera train writes a warning on standard error whenever training stops this way, after any number of iterations.
  • The line search of an iteration failed far from the optimum; the model keeps the best weights of the run, and lindera train writes a warning on standard error. A search direction with a component that is not finite, which the optimizer builds from a step that left the gradient unchanged, fails the line search too (#1301).
  • max-iterations was reached before the objective converged.

lindera train prints which one stopped it, with the number of iterations and of evaluations, each evaluation being one forward-backward pass over every lattice; with the files in resources/training/:

L-BFGS stopped after 8 iterations and 9 evaluations of the loss and its gradient: converged

Required Input Files

1. Seed Lexicon (seed.csv)

Base vocabulary dictionary in MeCab CSV format.

外国,0,0,0,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,外国,ガイコク,ガイコク
人,0,0,0,名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,人,ジン,ジン
参政,0,0,0,名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,参政,サンセイ,サンセイ

Each line contains: surface,left_id,right_id,cost,pos,pos_detail1,pos_detail2,pos_detail3,inflection_type,inflection_form,base_form,reading,pronunciation

The left_id, right_id, and cost fields are set to 0 in the seed dictionary -- the trainer will compute appropriate values from the CRF model.

The seed lexicon is read as CSV, as lindera build reads lex.csv:

  • A field may be quoted, as mecab-ko-dic's comma surface is: ",",1792,3558,788,SC,*,*,*,*,*,*,*.
  • A line that starts with # is a row, not a comment, as UniDic's # surface is. Blank lines and rows with fewer than five fields are skipped.
  • The feature of a row is the text after its fourth field, as written, quotes included. lindera export writes it back as it is, and quotes a surface that contains ,, " or a line break.
  • A quoted field that spans lines is an error that names the line. It is most likely a quote that is never closed, which would otherwise swallow the rows after it.
  • The rows keep their order, which gives their labels their ids.

To read the columns of a feature, for the rewrite rules, the feature templates and unknown-word matching, lindera train splits it as MeCab's learner does (tokenizeCSV), not as the CSV reader above does. The features of the corpus are split the same way.

  • A quoted column is one column, with "" read as ". The definition of mecab-jieba's 4S店, "authorized full-service car dealership (offering sales, spare parts, after-sales service and customer support)", is one column.
  • Spaces and tabs before a column are skipped: CC-CEDICT's COVID-19, the coronavirus disease identified in 2019/ is the two columns COVID-19 and the coronavirus disease identified in 2019/.
  • The text from a closing quote to the next , is dropped: "bamboo" radical in Chinese characters (Kangxi radical 118)/ is the column bamboo.
  • A , at the end of a feature does not start an empty last column.

2. Training Corpus (corpus.txt)

Annotated text data in tab-separated format. Each line is surface<TAB>pos_info, and sentences are separated by EOS.

外国	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,外国,ガイコク,ガイコク
人	名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,人,ジン,ジン
参政	名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,参政,サンセイ,サンセイ
権	名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,権,ケン,ケン
EOS

これ	連体詞,*,*,*,*,*,これ,コレ,コレ
は	助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
テスト	名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,テスト,テスト,テスト
EOS

A gold token is a seed word only when a seed row has its surface and its whole feature string, as the seed lexicon writes it, quotes included. In the example above, each feature is that of the seed row with the same surface. A gold token whose feature differs in any column, the reading for instance, is learned as an unknown word or a virtual label, and the seed rows with its surface become negative examples at its position; lindera train warns when most gold tokens are like this (see How training works).

Training quality depends heavily on the quantity and quality of this corpus.

3. Character Definition (char.def)

Defines character type categories and Unicode code point ranges.

# Category definition: category_name compatibility_flag continuity_flag length
DEFAULT 0 1 0
SPACE 0 1 0
HIRAGANA 1 1 0
KATAKANA 1 1 0
KANJI 0 0 2
ALPHA 1 1 0
NUMERIC 1 1 0

# Character range mapping
0x0020 SPACE             # Space (reserved for SPACE)
0x0009 SPACE             # Tab
0x000A SPACE             # Line feed
0x000B SPACE             # Vertical tab
0x000D SPACE             # Carriage return
0x3041..0x3096 HIRAGANA  # Hiragana
0x30A1..0x30F6 KATAKANA  # Katakana
0x4E00..0x9FAF KANJI     # Kanji
0x0030..0x0039 NUMERIC   # Numbers
0x0041..0x005A ALPHA     # Uppercase letters
0x0061..0x007A ALPHA     # Lowercase letters

Parameters control the unknown words that a character's default category creates: whether they are created even where a dictionary word starts (INVOKE), whether a run in which each character shares a category with the one before continues as a single token (GROUP), and up to which length shorter candidates are created (LENGTH).

A range line can list more than one category (for example 0x4E00 KANJINUMERIC KANJI), and every range line needs at least one. When several lines cover the same code point, the last line decides its categories, as in MeCab. The first category on that line is the character's default category: the only one that creates unknown-word candidates, and the one the %t feature template uses.

As in MeCab, a range line can name only categories defined on an earlier line, and each category is defined once. lindera train and lindera build reject a char.def that breaks either, with an error that names the line and the category. For example, lindera train with 0x30FC KATAKANA inserted as the first line of char.def, before the line that defines KATAKANA:

Error: LinderaError { kind: Args, source: failed to parse char.def: LinderaError(kind=Content, source=char.def: line 1: category KATAKANA is not defined; a range line can only name a category defined on an earlier line) }

Keep the SPACE category, which MeCab requires in every char.def along with DEFAULT, and its line in unk.def: every category needs at least one unk.def line (see the next section). The segmenter treats its characters as whitespace: by default it skips them, as MeCab does, and does not output them. Without --keep-whitespace, a dictionary whose char.def has no SPACE category cannot be used: lindera tokenize fails with SPACE category is not defined in the dictionary (char.def).

Training creates the unknown-word candidates with the runtime's own code (Lattice::unknown_word_candidates), so it learns weights for the candidates that the built dictionary produces:

  • At each position, the character's default category creates the candidates. It creates none when its INVOKE is 0 and a seed word starts there.
  • With GROUP 1, the run in which each character shares a category with the one before becomes one candidate.
  • With LENGTH n, the candidates of 1 to n characters are created too, while each character shares a category with the first one (the length ladder). In the example above, KANJI 0 0 2 gives a kanji where no seed word starts the candidates of one and two kanji.
  • Each unk.def entry of the category gets every one of these spans.

Grouping is unbounded, as at runtime by default. The Rust API's Trainer::max_grouping_len caps it with the runtime's meaning (characters beyond the first); the CLI has no option for it.

4. Unknown Word Definition (unk.def)

Defines the unknown words that each character category creates. Each line is category,left_id,right_id,cost,feature..., where category is a category name from char.def. As in the seed lexicon, the ids and the cost are set to 0; export writes the trained values.

# Unknown word definitions
DEFAULT,0,0,0,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
SPACE,0,0,0,記号,空白,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
HIRAGANA,0,0,0,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
KATAKANA,0,0,0,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
KANJI,0,0,0,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
ALPHA,0,0,0,名詞,固有名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*
NUMERIC,0,0,0,名詞,数,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
  • Every line is an entry of its own, and a category can have several: one for each part of speech its unknown words can take. mecab-ipadic's unk.def, for example, has 40 lines for 11 categories, six of them for KANJI (名詞,一般, 名詞,サ変接続 and four kinds of 名詞,固有名詞).
  • Each entry becomes a CRF label of its own, whose %t is the id of its category. A candidate of the category is created once for each entry, so training learns which entry fits where.
  • The order of the lines is kept: lindera export writes one line for each entry, in the same order.
  • Lines that start with # and empty lines are skipped. A line with fewer than five fields (the category, the two ids, the cost and at least one feature column) is an error:
Error: LinderaError { kind: Args, source: unk.def line 1: expected at least 5 fields (category, left id, right id, cost, feature), got 4 }
  • As in MeCab, every line names a category that char.def defines, and every category of char.def has at least one line. lindera train and lindera build reject an unk.def that breaks either. The error names the category and, for a line whose category char.def does not define, the line, counted with the comment and empty lines. For example, lindera train with SYMBOL,0,0,0,記号,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,* appended to the unk.def above as its ninth line, while char.def has no SYMBOL category:
Error: LinderaError { kind: Args, source: failed to check unk.def: LinderaError(kind=Content, source=unk.def: line 9: category SYMBOL is not defined in char.def) }

5. Feature Template (feature.def)

MeCab-compatible feature extraction patterns that define what information the CRF model uses for learning.

# Unigram features (word-level)
UNIGRAM U00:%F[0]           # POS
UNIGRAM U01:%F[0],%F?[1]    # POS + POS detail (%F?[n] = optional, skipped if *)
UNIGRAM U02:%F[6]           # Base form
UNIGRAM U03:%w              # Surface form

# Bigram features (context combination)
BIGRAM B00:%L[0]/%R[0]      # Left POS / Right POS
BIGRAM B01:%L[0],%L[1]/%R[0],%R[1]  # Left POS detail / Right POS detail

Template variables:

VariableDescription
%F[n] / %F?[n]Feature field at index n (? = optional, skipped if value is *)
%L[n]Left context feature field (from rewrite.def left section)
%R[n]Right context feature field (from rewrite.def right section)
%wSurface form of the word
%uUnigram rewritten feature string
%lLeft rewritten feature string
%rRight rewritten feature string

The fields of %F[n], %L[n] and %R[n] are the columns of the rewritten features, split as described in Seed Lexicon. %u, %l and %r are the rewritten features as rewrite.def writes them, with a column that contains , or " quoted.

A template that reads past the last column of a feature gives no feature for it, with or without ?, as in MeCab's learner. For example, UNIGRAM U06:%F[6] gives nothing for the unk.def feature n,*,*,*,*, which has five columns. A bigram template gives nothing when either %L[n] or %R[n] reads past the last column.

6. Feature Rewrite Rules (rewrite.def)

Feature normalization rules in MeCab-compatible 3-section format. Sections are separated by blank lines.

# Section 1: Unigram rewrite rules
名詞,固有名詞,*  名詞,固有名詞
助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・デス  助動詞
*  *

# Section 2: Left context rewrite rules
名詞,固有名詞,*  名詞,固有名詞
助詞,*  助詞
*  *

# Section 3: Right context rewrite rules
名詞,固有名詞,*  名詞,固有名詞
助詞,*  助詞
*  *

Each line is pattern<TAB>replacement. Patterns use * as a wildcard and are matched by prefix. The first matching rule in each section is applied. Different rules can be applied to unigram, left context, and right context independently, enabling fine-grained feature normalization to reduce sparsity.

The pattern, the replacement and the feature are split into columns as described in Seed Lexicon, so a quoted column with , in it is one column. As MeCab does, the rewritten columns are joined with ,, and a column that contains , or " is quoted, with its quotes doubled: with the left rule * $5, the feature n,dian4,店,店,"shop, store",1 is rewritten to "shop, store".

Training Parameters

ParameterDescriptionDefault
lambdaRegularization coefficient (controls overfitting), finite and >= 0; with l2, MeCab's -c C is 1 / C1.0
regularizationRegularization type: l1, l2, or elasticnet, in any case (elastic_net and elastic-net also select Elastic Net)l2
elastic-net-l1-ratioL1 ratio for Elastic Net regularization (0.0-1.0, only used with --regularization elasticnet)0.5
max-iterationsMaximum number of training iterations, 1 or more100
etaTolerance of the convergence test (see How training works); 0 disables the test0.00005
max-threadsNumber of parallel processing threads, 1 or moreCPU core count

A lambda of 0 disables regularization for every type. For Elastic Net, a ratio of 0 uses only L2, and a ratio of 1 uses only L1.

The defaults are those of MeCab's learner: L2 regularization with lambda 1.0 is its objective with -c 1.0. On the mecab-ipadic cross-validation data of #1110, they score as MeCab's learner does and converge in about as many iterations, 77 to 82 (#1261, #1290): boundary F1 0.9613 and span + POS (4 columns) F1 0.9397 on average over 5 folds, where v6's default settings, L1 with lambda 0.01, reached max-iterations on every fold with 0.9578 and 0.9350. L1 sets many weights to 0, and lindera export gives labels with equal weights one context ID, so the L1 matrix.def is smaller: 8.3 MB there against 18.9 MB with L2, which makes the built dictionary 4.0 % larger. Training there takes about twice as long as MeCab's learner, and about two thirds of the time is spent outside the optimizer: before it starts (#1263) and after it stops.

CLI Usage

Train

lindera train \
    --seed seed.csv \
    --corpus corpus.txt \
    --char-def char.def \
    --unk-def unk.def \
    --feature-def feature.def \
    --rewrite-def rewrite.def \
    --max-iterations 100 \
    --max-threads 4 \
    --output model.dat

Export

Convert the trained model into dictionary source files:

lindera export \
    --model model.dat \
    --metadata metadata.json \
    --output ./dict-source

This produces the following files:

FileDescription
lex.csvLexicon with trained costs
matrix.defConnection cost matrix over every context ID, plus 0 for BOS/EOS, even when regularization leaves no bigram weight. A connection without a trained weight costs 0, as in training and in MeCab
unk.defUnknown word definition: one line for each input unk.def entry, in input order, with its category, trained IDs and cost, and feature
char.defCharacter definition
feature.defFeature template
rewrite.defFeature rewrite rules
left-id.defLeft context ID mapping
right-id.defRight context ID mapping
metadata.jsonDictionary metadata; its model_info.connection_matrix_size is the size of matrix.def, rows (right IDs) by columns (left IDs)

For example, if the unk.def above has a second KANJI line, KANJI,0,0,0,名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,*,*,*, after the first one, the exported unk.def keeps both, in input order:

DEFAULT,1,1,31699,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
SPACE,10,7,0,記号,空白,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
HIRAGANA,1,1,31699,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
KATAKANA,1,1,31699,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
KANJI,1,1,31699,名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
KANJI,3,3,4179,名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
ALPHA,11,10,10957,名詞,固有名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,*,*
NUMERIC,11,10,10957,名詞,数,*,*,*,*,*,*,*

Build

Compile the exported source files into a binary dictionary:

lindera build \
    --src ./dict-source \
    --dest ./dict-compiled \
    --metadata ./dict-source/metadata.json

lindera build checks that the context IDs of every lex.csv row and unk.def line lie inside matrix.def, as MeCab's mecab-dict-index does (see Context ID check). The files that lindera export writes pass this check.

Tokenize

Tokenize text with the built dictionary:

echo "これは外国人参政権です。" | lindera tokenize -d ./dict-compiled

With the files in resources/training/ as the inputs above, the output is:

これ	名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,これ,コレ,コレ
は	助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
外国	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,外国,ガイコク,ガイコク
人	名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,人,ジン,ジン
参政	名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,参政,サンセイ,サンセイ
権	名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,権,ケン,ケン
です	助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・デス,基本形,です,デス,デス
。	記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。
EOS

A space in the input, as in これは 外国人参政権です。, is skipped and gives the same output. With --keep-whitespace, it is output as the SPACE unknown word:

これ	名詞,代名詞,一般,*,*,*,これ,コレ,コレ
は	助詞,係助詞,*,*,*,*,は,ハ,ワ
 	記号,空白,*,*,*,*,*,*,*
外国	名詞,一般,*,*,*,*,外国,ガイコク,ガイコク
人	名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,人,ジン,ジン
参政	名詞,サ変接続,*,*,*,*,参政,サンセイ,サンセイ
権	名詞,接尾,一般,*,*,*,権,ケン,ケン
です	助動詞,*,*,*,特殊・デス,基本形,です,デス,デス
。	記号,句点,*,*,*,*,。,。,。
EOS

Output Model Format

The trained model is serialized in rkyv binary format for fast loading. It contains:

  • Feature weights learned by the CRF
  • Label set (the seed rows, then the unk.def entries)
  • Part-of-speech information
  • The unk.def entries, in file order, and the content of char.def, feature.def and rewrite.def
  • Training metadata (format version, the regularization coefficient, type and Elastic Net ratio, iterations, feature/label counts)

The format version is 3.0.0 (lindera_trainer::model::MODEL_FORMAT_VERSION), and it changes whenever the layout or the meaning of the model changes. lindera export rejects a model.dat written by another version, including every model.dat written before 7.0.0, with an error that ends in "re-run lindera train to regenerate it". Train such a model again with the current version.

The output is byte-reproducible: training the same inputs twice with the same flags produces identical model.dat bytes, so the artifact can be checksummed and diffed. This holds for any --max-threads value: the gradient and the loss are summed over a fixed partition of the training data in a fixed order, so the thread count changes only how long training takes, never its result.

API Usage

For the full lindera-trainer API surface, see Lindera Trainer Architecture and API Reference.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::fs::File;
use lindera_trainer::{Corpus, Trainer, TrainerConfig};

// Load configuration from files
let seed_file = File::open("resources/training/seed.csv")?;
let char_file = File::open("resources/training/char.def")?;
let unk_file = File::open("resources/training/unk.def")?;
let feature_file = File::open("resources/training/feature.def")?;
let rewrite_file = File::open("resources/training/rewrite.def")?;

let config = TrainerConfig::from_readers(
    seed_file,
    char_file,
    unk_file,
    feature_file,
    rewrite_file
)?;

// Initialize and configure trainer
let trainer = Trainer::new(config)?
    .max_iter(100)
    .num_threads(4);

// Load corpus
let corpus_file = File::open("resources/training/corpus.txt")?;
let corpus = Corpus::from_reader(corpus_file)?;

// Execute training
let model = trainer.train(corpus)?;

// Save model (binary format)
let mut output = File::create("trained_model.dat")?;
model.write_model(&mut output)?;

// Output in Lindera dictionary format. output_user.csv holds the entries
// loaded by read_user_lexicon, in input order; without that call it is empty.
let mut lex_out = File::create("output_lex.csv")?;
let mut conn_out = File::create("output_conn.dat")?;
let mut unk_out = File::create("output_unk.def")?;
let mut user_out = File::create("output_user.csv")?;
model.write_dictionary(&mut lex_out, &mut conn_out, &mut unk_out, &mut user_out)?;

Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
}

Recommended Corpus Specifications

For generating effective dictionaries for real applications:

Corpus Size

LevelSentencesUse Case
Minimum100+Basic operation verification
Recommended1,000+Practical applications
Ideal10,000+Commercial quality

Quality Guidelines

  • Vocabulary diversity: Balanced distribution of different parts of speech, coverage of inflections and suffixes, appropriate inclusion of technical terms and proper nouns.
  • Consistency: Apply analysis criteria consistently across the corpus.
  • Verification: Manually verify morphological analysis results. Maintain an error rate below 5%.

Contributing

Thank you for your interest in contributing to Lindera! This page provides guidelines to help you get started.

Getting Started

  1. Fork the repository on GitHub.

  2. Clone your fork locally:

    git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/lindera.git
cd lindera

  3. Create a feature branch:

    git checkout -b feature/my-feature

  4. Make your changes, then verify they pass all checks:

    cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy -- -D warnings
cargo test
make check-docs

    Note: CI enforces all four: it checks formatting, runs clippy (warnings as errors) and the tests for each crate with the features it tests that crate with, and fails on rustdoc warnings in any crate. make check-docs leaves out the language bindings, which need their languages' toolchains to build; if you change one, also run make check-docs-lindera-<binding>, as that binding's CI job does. make lint and make test apply the same per-crate features, and make lint-lindera-<binding> also runs the language-side linter that the binding's CI job runs. make lint ends with make lint-scripts, which lints the scripts outside the crates as the Lint scripts CI job does; see Build & Test.

  5. Commit and push your changes, then open a pull request.

Code Style

  • Follow the existing code style in the repository.
  • Run cargo fmt before committing.
  • All public and private items (types, functions, modules, fields, constants, type aliases) must have documentation comments (///).
  • Trait implementation methods should also have documentation comments describing implementation-specific behavior.
  • Function and method documentation should include # Arguments and # Returns sections where applicable. CI fails on these sections under the Japanese names # 引数 and # 戻り値.
  • Code comments, documentation comments, commit messages, log messages, and error messages should be written in English.
  • Avoid unwrap() and expect() in production code (test code is fine).
  • Use unsafe blocks only when necessary, and always include a // SAFETY: ... comment.
  • Use file-based module style (src/tokenizer.rs) instead of mod.rs style.

Language Binding Parity

Lindera ships bindings for Python, Node.js, Ruby, PHP, and WASM. When adding or reviewing a binding feature, apply the following policy:

  • Keep the feature set aligned. Capabilities — tokenization (tokenize / tokenize_surfaces / tokenize_nbest), user dictionaries, character filters, and token filters — should be available in every binding. A feature added to one binding should come with a plan (or a tracking issue) for the others.
  • Let representation and lifetime management follow each language. Whether tokens are class instances or plain data, naming conventions (camelCase vs. snake_case), and serialization helpers (to_dict / to_h / toArray / toJSON) are per-language decisions and do not need to match across bindings. The JS bindings return plain objects because their hosts defer class finalizers, while Python, Ruby, and PHP keep classes because their finalization is deterministic.

Put shared logic in lindera-binding (e.g. TokenView) so each binding only maps core data into its FFI types.

Testing

  • Write unit tests for all new functionality.

  • Run the relevant test(s) during development for fast feedback:

    cargo test -p <crate> <test_name>

  • When working on training pipeline functionality, run the lindera-trainer crate's tests:

    cargo test -p lindera-trainer

Commit Messages

Follow the Conventional Commits specification. Write commit messages in English.

Examples:

  • feat: add Korean dictionary support
  • fix: correct character category ID in trainer
  • docs: update installation instructions
  • refactor: split large training method into smaller functions

Documentation

  • If your change affects user-facing documentation, update the relevant files in docs/src/.

  • After editing Markdown files, verify there are no lint errors:

    markdownlint-cli2 "docs/src/**/*.md"

  • Rules are configured in .markdownlint.json at the repository root.

Dependencies

When adding new dependencies, verify license compatibility. Lindera uses the MIT / Apache-2.0 dual license.

Feature Flags

Use #[cfg(feature = "train")] for conditional compilation of training-related code. See Feature Flags for a full list.

Reporting Issues

When reporting a bug, please include:

  • Lindera version (lindera --version or check Cargo.toml)
  • Rust version (rustc --version)
  • Operating system
  • Steps to reproduce the issue
  • Expected and actual behavior
